title: Seasons in India: summer, monsoon and winter, and what changes

summary.text: Every year in India, a hot summer, a rainy monsoon and a cooler winter come round in the same order. These parts of the year are called seasons. In each season the heat, the rain and the wind change. People, other animals and plants change too: what we wear, what we eat, which birds call and which trees flower. The seasons do not come at the same time all over India. In this unit your child finds out what changes in each season, and tests why white clothes are cooler in the summer sun.
summary.art: A long strip picture of one Indian street in three parts: a hot summer afternoon with a red gulmohar tree and a buttermilk stall, a rainy monsoon day with umbrellas and puddles, and a misty winter morning with people in sweaters.

intro.hook: In May in Chennai, a white cotton saree and a black T-shirt hang on the same clothes line. After an hour in the sun, the black T-shirt is too hot to touch, and the saree is not. Both were in the same sunshine. Why did one get so much hotter?
intro.text: Look at a photo of your home from a few months ago. Is anything different from today? Maybe the fan was off, or there was an umbrella by the door, or everyone wore sweaters. The year in India turns from hot to rainy to cool, and back again. These parts of the year are called seasons. In this unit we find out what changes in each season, why the monsoon reaches Kochi weeks before Delhi, and why people choose white cotton for the summer.
intro.art: A black T-shirt and a white cotton saree hanging side by side on a clothes line on a sunny Chennai balcony, with a girl touching the T-shirt and pulling her hand back.

outcomes: By the end I can name India's three big seasons, summer, monsoon and winter, in the order they come.
By the end I can say what changes in each season: the heat, the rain, the wind and the clothes we wear.
By the end I can say that the seasons come at different times in different parts of India, with one example.
By the end I can show with my own test that a black cloth takes in more sunlight than a white one, and so gets warmer.
By the end I can give two examples of how other animals and plants change with the seasons.
By the end I can read a calendar and count how many months each season lasts where I live.

terms.meaning: A season is a part of the year with its own kind of weather. The seasons come back in the same order every year.
terms.example: In most of India, summer comes before the monsoon, and winter comes after it.
terms.art: A circle split into three coloured parts: orange for summer, blue for monsoon and pale grey-green for winter, with a small sun, a raincloud and a woollen cap.

terms.meaning: Summer is the hottest season. In most of India it comes from March to May or June.
terms.example: In summer, mangoes come to the market and the fan runs all night.
terms.art: A hot afternoon street with a mango cart and a girl drinking buttermilk under an umbrella.

terms.meaning: The monsoon is the rainy season. A strong wind from the sea brings big clouds and heavy rain. The word comes from the Arabic word mawsim, which means season.
terms.example: In Kerala, the monsoon rain usually starts around the first of June.
terms.art: Dark clouds over coconut trees on a Kerala beach, with heavy rain and children running with umbrellas.

terms.meaning: Winter is the coolest season. In most of India it comes from December to February.
terms.example: In Delhi, winter mornings are cold and foggy. In Chennai, winter is only a little cooler than the rest of the year.
terms.art: A foggy morning street in Delhi with people in sweaters and shawls, and a tea stall with steam rising.

terms.meaning: Temperature is how hot or cold something is.
terms.example: The temperature of a cup of tea is high. The temperature of an ice cube is low.
terms.art: A steaming cup of tea next to an ice cube on a plate.

terms.meaning: Humid air holds a lot of water that you cannot see. Humid air feels sticky, and wet clothes dry slowly in it.
terms.example: In Mumbai in July, the air is so humid that clothes take two days to dry.
terms.art: Damp clothes on a line indoors in Mumbai, with rain outside the window and a boy touching a still-wet shirt.

terms.meaning: To absorb light means to take it in. Light that is absorbed turns into heat.
terms.example: A black T-shirt absorbs most of the sunlight that falls on it, so it gets hot.
terms.art: Yellow sun rays going into a black T-shirt and wavy heat lines rising from it.

terms.meaning: To reflect light means to send it back. A white surface reflects most of the light that falls on it.
terms.example: A white wall reflects so much sunlight that it hurts your eyes at noon.
terms.art: Yellow sun rays bouncing off a white wall.

terms.meaning: The northeast monsoon is the second rainy season of South-East India. It brings rain to Tamil Nadu and nearby places from October to December.
terms.example: Chennai gets most of its rain in October, November and December, not in July.
terms.art: A map of South India with a blue arrow coming from the north-east across the sea to Chennai, and rain clouds over the city.

explanations.context: This card is about what we mean by a season.
explanations.definition: A season is a part of the year with its own kind of weather. The seasons come back in the same order every year.
explanations.description: Weather is what the air is doing today: hot or cool, rainy or dry, windy or still. A season is the usual weather for many weeks in a row. One cool day in May does not make winter. The seasons come in a cycle. A cycle is something that happens again and again in the same order, like the days of the week.
examples: In Hyderabad, April and May are hot almost every day. That is the summer season.
In Mumbai, it rains on most days of July. That is the monsoon season.
Days of the week come in a cycle, and so do the seasons.
explanations.art: A circle of three pictures joined by arrows: a hot sun, a raincloud and a foggy morning, going round and round.

explanations.context: This card is about the three seasons most people in India talk about.
explanations.definition: Most of India has three big seasons: a hot summer, a rainy monsoon and a cooler winter.
explanations.description: In most of India, summer comes from March to May. It is the hottest time, and often dry. The monsoon comes from June to September, with a wet wind from the sea and heavy rain. Winter comes from December to February, with cool nights, and very cold mornings in the north.
examples: Summer: hot days, mangoes, buttermilk, the fan on all night.
Monsoon: heavy rain, puddles, frogs croaking, clothes that will not dry.
Winter: cool mornings, sweaters and blankets, oranges and groundnut chikki.
explanations.art: Three panels of the same balcony: bright sun and a dry potted plant, heavy rain and an umbrella, and a misty morning with a shawl on the chair.

explanations.concept: Why summer is the hottest season
explanations.context: This card is about why summer is hotter than winter.
explanations.definition: In summer, the Sun climbs higher in the sky at midday and stays up longer, so more sunlight reaches the ground each day.
explanations.description: In summer, the Sun rises earlier and sets later, so there are more hours of sunlight. At midday it is high in the sky. In winter, the Sun stays lower and the days are shorter. Sunlight for more hours, from higher up, heats the ground and the air more.
examples: In May, it is still light at 6.30 in the evening in most of India. In December, it is often dark by 6.
At noon in May, your shadow is very short, because the Sun is high.
In December, the midday Sun is lower, and your noon shadow is longer.
explanations.art: Two pictures of a girl on a terrace at noon: in May with the Sun high above and a tiny shadow, in December with the Sun lower and a longer shadow.

explanations.concept: The seasons come at different times across India
explanations.context: This card is about why it can be raining in one Indian city and sunny in another in the same week.
explanations.definition: India is a big country, so the seasons do not start or end on the same day everywhere.
explanations.description: The monsoon rain usually reaches Kerala first, around the first of June. Then it moves north. It reaches Mumbai about ten days later, and most of India by early July. Chennai gets most of its rain from October to December, from a wind called the northeast monsoon.
examples: In early June, it may be pouring in Kochi while Delhi is still very hot and dry.
In November, Chennai may have heavy rain while Mumbai is dry and sunny.
In January, Leh in Ladakh can be far below freezing, while Thiruvananthapuram is warm.
explanations.art: A map of India with a blue arrow of monsoon clouds starting at Kerala and moving north, a small sun over Delhi, snow over Ladakh and heavy rain over Meghalaya.

explanations.concept: Why a black cloth gets hotter in the sun
explanations.context: This card is about the Black or White test, where you put ice under two cloths in the sun.
explanations.definition: A black cloth absorbs most of the sunlight that falls on it, and that light turns into heat. A white cloth reflects most of the light back.
explanations.description: Sunlight carries energy. A black cloth sends back very little light, so it takes in almost all of it, and that energy turns into heat. A white cloth sends back most of the light. So in the same sun, a black cloth gets hotter than a white one, and ice under it melts faster.
examples: A black car seat in the sun can be too hot to sit on. A white seat in the same sun is cooler.
In Ahmedabad, women in many homes have painted their tin roofs white to keep their rooms cooler in summer.
Many people in Kerala wear a white or cream mundu or saree on hot days.
explanations.art: Sun rays falling on a black cloth and a white cloth side by side. The rays go into the black cloth, and bounce off the white cloth.

explanations.concept: What changes for people in each season
explanations.context: This card is about how families change what they do as the seasons turn.
explanations.definition: People change their clothes, food, work and festivals with the seasons.
explanations.description: In summer, people wear loose cotton, drink buttermilk and coconut water, and stay in the shade at noon. In the monsoon, people bring out umbrellas and raincoats and eat hot roasted corn, and farmers sow rice and many other crops. In winter, sweaters and blankets come out of the cupboard. Festivals follow the seasons too. Onam comes in Kerala in August or September. Pongal, Makar Sankranti, Uttarayan in Gujarat and Magh Bihu in Assam all come in January.
examples: Neer mor, a thin spiced buttermilk, is given out free at street stalls in Tamil Nadu in summer.
Roasted corn, called bhutta in many places, is sold hot on rainy days.
In January, the sky over Ahmedabad fills with kites for Uttarayan.
explanations.art: Three small scenes: a neer mor stall in summer, a corn seller with a coal fire under an umbrella in the rain, and kites over rooftops in Ahmedabad in January.

explanations.concept: What changes for other animals and plants
explanations.context: This card is about how birds, frogs, insects and trees change with the seasons.
explanations.definition: Other animals and plants sense the season and change what they do.
explanations.description: In summer, the male koel calls 'koo-oo, koo-oo' again and again, to call female koels. It is the season when koels breed, which means have young ones. In the monsoon, male frogs croak loudly by the puddles to call females, and peacocks spread their tails and dance for peahens. Trees change too: gulmohar trees cover themselves in red flowers in April and May, and the konna tree hangs out yellow flowers in time for Vishu in Kerala.
examples: The koel's call is one of the loudest sounds of an Indian summer morning.
After the first heavy rain, frogs that hid underground all summer come out and croak.
Mango trees flower in winter and spring, and the fruit is ready in summer.
explanations.art: A male koel, glossy black with red eyes, calling from a branch, a frog croaking with a puffed throat by a puddle, and a peacock dancing in the rain.

explanations.concept: How many seasons does India have?
explanations.context: This card is about a question people answer in different ways.
explanations.description: Most people say India has three seasons. But there are other good ways to count them, and each one fits some part of the year better.
examples: The India Meteorological Department, which forecasts India's weather, uses four seasons.
The old Sanskrit calendar has six seasons, called ritus.
Old Tamil books also count six seasons, with names like Kaar for the rains and Ilavenil for the warm season.

perspectives.explanation: There are three seasons: summer, monsoon and winter. That is what most of us feel.
There are four: winter (January and February), summer (March to May, which it calls the pre-monsoon season), the monsoon (June to September), and the season after the monsoon (October to December).

perspectives.who: The old Sanskrit and Tamil calendars
perspectives.explanation: There are six, about two months each. Spring, summer, the rains, early autumn, the dewy season and the cold season each have their own name.

explanations.art: Three circles side by side, cut into three, four and six slices, each slice with a tiny picture of its weather.

agreed.text: Most of India has a hot summer, a rainy monsoon and a cooler winter, in the same order every year.
agreed.evidence: The India Meteorological Department has measured the heat and rain in Indian cities every day for about 150 years. The pattern comes back every year.

agreed.text: The monsoon rain reaches different parts of India at different times.
agreed.evidence: Every year, the weather department marks the day the rains begin in each place. Kerala is usually first, around the first of June.

agreed.text: A black surface absorbs more sunlight than a white one, so it gets hotter in the same sun.
agreed.evidence: You can feel it on a black and a white cloth in the sun. Ice under a black cloth melts faster.

agreed.text: Many other animals and plants breed, flower or fruit in a particular season.
agreed.evidence: People who watch birds, frogs and trees have written down for many years when each one calls, breeds or flowers.

challenging.claim: It is the same season all over India at the same time.
challenging.for: Calendars and school books often list one set of months for each season.
challenging.against: In November, Chennai gets heavy rain while Mumbai is dry. In January, Ladakh is freezing while Kerala is warm. The monsoon reaches Kerala weeks before it reaches Delhi.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the seasons are the same everywhere in India.

challenging.claim: Black clothes always make you hotter in the sun.
challenging.who: A common idea, tested by scientists in 1980
challenging.for: A black cloth absorbs more sunlight and gets hotter. The Black or White test shows this: ice under a black cloth melts faster than ice under a white cloth.
challenging.against: Scientists measured Bedouin people in the desert wearing loose black and white robes. The black robe got hotter on the outside, but the person inside gained about the same heat. Moving air carried the extra heat away before it reached the skin.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the colour of clothes is the whole story.

challenging.claim: A peacock dances to bring the rain.
challenging.who: An old saying in many parts of India
challenging.for: Peacocks dance most in the rainy months, often when clouds gather.
challenging.against: A male peacock dances to show his tail to peahens. His dancing season is the breeding season, which in most of India falls during the monsoon. The rain comes from the wind and the clouds, with or without the dance.
challenging.context: This card is about why peacocks dance in the monsoon.

challenging.claim: The monsoon is a giant sea breeze. In summer the land gets hotter than the sea, so wet wind blows from the sea onto the land.
challenging.who: Edmond Halley, a British scientist, in 1686, and many school books since
challenging.for: In summer, the land does get much hotter than the sea, and the monsoon wind does blow from the sea.
challenging.against: Many weather scientists today say this is only part of the story. They say the whole belt of rain near the middle of the Earth moves north in summer, following the Sun, and India's mountains help to pull it in.
challenging.context: This card is about what makes the monsoon come.

big_questions.q: If the seasons come at different times in Kochi and in Delhi, when does the monsoon really begin?
big_questions.hint: Is there one start day for all of India, or a start day for each place?

big_questions.q: In the Black or White test, a black cloth and a white cloth sit in the same sunshine. Why do they end up at different temperatures?
big_questions.hint: Think about how much of the light each cloth took in.

big_questions.q: A koel calls in summer and a frog croaks in the monsoon. How do they know which season it is?
big_questions.hint: What could they feel or notice: the heat, the rain, the length of the day?

big_questions.q: A year is one trip of the Earth round the Sun, and the seasons come back every year. Do you also have seasons in your own life?
big_questions.hint: Think of things you do only in one part of the year, and things that come back.

big_questions.q: Some people count three seasons, and some count six. Who is right?
big_questions.hint: Can there be more than one good way to cut the same year into parts?

story.title: Ammamma and the First Day of June
story.note: A made-up story. It is true that the monsoon rain usually reaches Kerala around the first of June and Mumbai about ten days later, that Chennai gets most of its rain from October to December, that the konna tree flowers for Vishu in April, and that schools in Kerala open in early June.
text: Ammu lived on the sixth floor of a building in Kochi, in Kerala. She lived with her Amma, her little brother Kannan and their grandmother, Ammamma. Ammu was seven. Kannan was five.
It was the end of May. The air was hot and sticky, even at night. The fan spun all the time. Kannan lay on the cool floor tiles and said, "I am melting like ice cream."
Ammamma laughed. She was hanging her white cotton saree on the balcony line. "Not long now," she said. "The rain is coming."
"How do you know?" asked Ammu.

"Come and look," said Ammamma. She pointed out over the rooftops to the sea. "See the clouds? Last week the sky was empty and white. Now big grey clouds are piling up over the sea. And feel the wind."
Ammu stood at the railing. A strong wind pushed her hair back. It smelled of salt. "It is coming from the sea," she said.
"Yes," said Ammamma. "In the monsoon, the wind blows in from the sea, and it carries the rain."

Kannan came out in his black T-shirt, his favourite one. He touched the railing and pulled his hand back. Then he touched his own T-shirt. "My shirt is hot!" he said. He touched Ammamma's white saree on the line. "Your saree is not so hot. Why?"
"Good question," said Ammamma. "Ammu, what do you think?"
Ammu thought. "They are in the same sun," she said. "So it must be the colour. We could test it."
"Tomorrow," said Ammamma. "With two cloths and two ice cubes. Today, let us watch the sky."
That evening, Amma's phone rang. It was Shabnam aunty, Amma's friend, calling from Chennai. Ammu shouted into the phone, "Aunty, is the rain coming to you too?"
Shabnam aunty laughed. "Not yet, Ammu! Here it is hot and sunny. We get a few showers in summer, but our big rains come in October and November."
Kannan frowned. "But the rain is coming now," he said. "Ammamma said so."

"The rain is coming to Kochi," said Ammamma gently. "India is very big, Kannan. The monsoon rain reaches Kerala first. Then it travels north, slowly, like a long train of clouds. It reaches Mumbai about ten days later. Chennai gets its big rain later in the year, from a different wind."
"So it is not the same season everywhere?" asked Kannan.
"Not on the same day," said Ammamma.
The next morning was the first of June. Ammu woke up early. The light was grey, not bright. The air smelled different. Then she heard a sound on the window, tap, tap, tap. Then it became a roar.
"It's raining!" she shouted.
Everyone ran to the balcony. Rain came down in thick grey sheets. The coconut trees bent in the wind. The road below turned into a brown river. The air was suddenly cool.
Kannan held out his hand and caught the rain. "It's cold!" he said. "I am not melting any more."
Ammamma brought her white saree in from the line, now soaking wet. "It will take two days to dry now," she said. "That is the monsoon too."
Ammu ran to get her notebook. On a fresh page she wrote the date, 1 June. She drew grey clouds, rain, and a small frog.
"Why a frog?" asked Kannan.
"Because tonight we will hear them," said Ammu. "Ammamma says the frogs come out when the rains come."
That night, from the puddles by the gate, came a loud croaking. Kannan sat up in bed. "How did the frogs know?" he asked.
"They felt the rain," said Ammamma. "They have been waiting underground all summer for it. Every living being in Kochi knows the season has turned: the frogs, the trees, and you."
Kannan thought about it. "Tomorrow is school," he said. "School always opens in the rain."
"Yes," said Amma. "New books, a new umbrella and wet socks. That is how Kerala starts the school year."
"And tomorrow," said Ammu, "we still have to do the ice test, inside by the window, when the sun comes out."
"If the sun comes out," said Ammamma, and she smiled.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Kannan first thinks the monsoon comes to all of India on the same day. Shabnam aunty's call and Ammamma's 'train of clouds' show him that the seasons arrive at different times in different places. The story also opens the question of why the black T-shirt was hotter than the white saree, which the child answers with their own test.
ask: How did Ammamma know the rain was coming?
Why was it not raining in Chennai when it rained in Kochi?
Why was Kannan's black T-shirt hotter than Ammamma's white saree?
What changed in Kochi on the day the monsoon came?

games.title: Pack for the Trip: a season and place card game
games.context: This is a packing game. Each card names a place in India and a month. You say what the weather will be like there, and what you would pack.

items.b: Winter. Freezing cold, with snow on the mountains. Pack a thick jacket, a woollen cap, gloves and warm socks.

items.f: Mumbai, Maharashtra, in August
items.b: Monsoon. Heavy rain, and the streets can flood. Pack an umbrella and a raincoat.

items.f: Delhi in January
items.b: Winter. Cold, foggy mornings. Pack a sweater, a shawl and socks.

items.b: Monsoon. Very wet and cool. Pack a raincoat and a light sweater.

items.f: Kolkata, West Bengal, in April
items.b: Summer. Hot and humid, with sudden evening storms. Pack cotton clothes and an umbrella.

items.f: Bengaluru, Karnataka, in December

items.b: Summer. Very hot and dry. Pack a cap, cotton clothes and a water bottle.

rules: Mix the trip cards and put them face down in a pile.
The first player takes the top card and reads out the place and the month. A grown-up can read it.
The player says the season there, and names two things to pack.
Turn the card over and read the back. If the season is right, the player gets 1 point. If both things to pack suit the weather, they get 1 more point.
Take turns until the pile is finished. The player with the most points wins. If points are equal, the players share the win.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. 2. If you have a map of India, put it where everyone can see. 3. Find Kochi, Chennai and Delhi on it together.
flow.say: Today we are going on trips all over India. Each card is a place and a month. Can you guess the weather before you pack?
flow.kid: Each card is a place and a month. Guess the weather. Then pack!
flow.parent: A map helps a lot. Any school atlas or a map on a phone will do.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to pick a card. 2. The player says the season and two things to pack. 3. Turn the card and give the points.
flow.say: Where are you going? What month? So what will the weather be like there? What will you pack?
flow.kid: Read your card. Say the season. Name two things to pack.

ask.q: The Chennai in May card and the Chennai in November card have different weather. Why?
good: May is summer there and very hot.
November is when Chennai gets its big rain.

flow.parent: Children often guess that it is cold in every city in January and rainy everywhere in July. Let the backs of the cards correct them, then point to the places on the map.

flow.do: Count the points. Then ask the last question.
flow.say: Which trip would you most like to go on? Why? What would you see there?
flow.kid: Which trip do you want most? Why?

check.q: Chennai gets its big rains in November. When does Mumbai get its big rains?
check.why: Mumbai gets its monsoon rain from June to September. Chennai gets its big rain later, from the northeast monsoon. If you chose November, look again at the Mumbai card.

rules: Put the three pile mats on the floor: summer, monsoon and winter.
Mix the 18 clue cards and split them into two equal piles, one for each player.
Say 'Go!' Each player puts their cards, clue side up, on the mat for the season they belong to, as fast as they can.
When both players have finished, turn every card over and check the back.

flow.do: Look at any card that went on the wrong mat. Talk about why.
flow.say: This one went on the wrong mat. What made you think of that season? Where would it go where you live?
flow.kid: Look at the cards on the wrong mat. Why did you put them there?
flow.parent: Some cards depend on where you live. Fog and seeing your breath belong to winter in the north, but rarely happen in Chennai. That is a good thing to notice, not a mistake.

check.q: Frogs are croaking all night by the puddles. Which season is it?
check.why: Male frogs croak loudly in the rainy season to call female frogs to the puddles. If you chose summer, remember that most frogs stay hidden underground in the dry, hot months.

experiments.title: Black or White: under which cloth does the ice melt first?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put two ice cubes in the sun. One is under a black cloth and one is under a white cloth. You find out which cloth takes in more of the sun's heat, and why people wear white in summer.
experiments.question: In the same sunshine, does ice melt faster under a black cloth or under a white cloth?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which ice cube will melt first: the one under the black cloth, the one under the white cloth, or will they melt at the same time? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use two ice cubes from the same tray, so they are the same size. We use two plates that are the same. The two cloths are about the same size and thickness. Both plates sit side by side in the same patch of sun for the same time. Only the colour of the cloth is different.
results_table: My guess: melts first or last?
How does the ice look after 15 minutes?
Spoons of water on the plate

materials.item: two ice cubes from the same ice tray
two steel plates or katoris of the same size
a black or very dark cloth, such as an old black T-shirt, a dark dupatta or a dark hanky, folded to the size of a hanky
a white cloth of about the same size and thickness, such as a white hanky or an old white vest
a sunny windowsill, a balcony or the building terrace with a grown-up, where the sun shines for at least 20 minutes
a teaspoon and a clock or phone timer

schedule.what: Guess, set the ice under the two cloths in the sun, feel the cloths, look after 15 minutes, count the spoons of water, and talk about why.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw the two plates after 15 minutes, with the ice you saw on each.

setup.art: Two steel plates side by side on a sunny windowsill, each with one ice cube from the same tray.
setup.caption: 1. Put one ice cube on each plate, side by side in the sun.

setup.art: One ice cube covered with a black cloth and the other with a white cloth, both lying flat over the ice in bright sunlight.
setup.caption: 2. Cover one with the black cloth and one with the white cloth.

setup.art: A child's palm resting lightly on top of the black cloth and then the white cloth.
setup.caption: 3. After 10 minutes, feel the top of each cloth.

setup.art: Both cloths lifted: a tiny piece of ice in a big puddle on the black plate, and a bigger ice cube in a small puddle on the white plate.
setup.caption: 4. After 15 minutes, lift the cloths and compare.

flow.do: 1. Draw the results table on paper. 2. Show your child the two cloths and the ice. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: We will put one ice cube under a black cloth and one under a white cloth, in the sun. Which one will melt first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One ice cube goes under black cloth, one under white. Which melts first? Why?

good: The black one, because black things get hot in the sun.
The white one, because white is brighter.
The same, because the sun is the same for both.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine if it has a reason. Do not explain yet. Let the ice answer.

flow.do: 1. Find a spot in direct sunshine. 2. Put the two plates side by side, a hand apart. 3. Put one ice cube on each plate. 4. Lay the black cloth over one cube and the white cloth over the other. 5. Note the time.
flow.say: Both plates are in the same sun. Only the cloth is different. Why does that matter?
flow.kid: Put both plates in the sun. Cover one ice cube with black and one with white.
flow.parent: Sunlight through a closed window works well. If the sun is behind clouds today, keep the ice in the freezer and try on the next sunny morning. On a terrace, stay with your child.

flow.do: 1. Wait. 2. After 10 minutes, your child lays a palm gently on top of each cloth, one after the other. 3. Write down which one feels warmer. 4. Keep waiting until 15 minutes have passed since you put the ice out.
flow.say: Do not lift the cloths yet. Touch the top of each one gently. Which feels warmer?
flow.kid: Touch the top of each cloth. Which one is warmer?

good: The black one.
The black one was quite hot. The white one was only a little warm.

flow.parent: In good sun, the black cloth feels clearly warmer within a few minutes. While you wait, read the explanation card India's three big seasons, or play one round of Three Piles.

flow.do: 1. After 15 minutes, lift both cloths. 2. Look at the two ice cubes and the water on each plate. 3. Draw what you see.
flow.say: Let us lift the cloths. Look at both ice cubes. What do you see?
flow.kid: Lift both cloths. Look at the ice. Which is smaller?
flow.parent: In strong sun, the ice under the black cloth is usually much smaller, or gone, with more water round it. The ice under the white cloth is still clearly there. If both are still large, cover them again and wait 10 more minutes. If both are already gone, try again next time with bigger cubes, or lift the cloths after 8 minutes.

flow.do: Count how many teaspoons of water you can scoop from each plate. Write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Let us count the water. Scoop it up with the teaspoon. How many spoons from each plate?
flow.kid: Scoop the water with a spoon. Count the spoons on each plate.
flow.parent: The cloths soak up a little meltwater, so count only the water on the plate, and lift the cloth to let it drip first. Both cloths do this, so the test stays fair. There will be only a few spoons of water, so also compare how big each ice cube looks.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child what they saw, and why they think it happened. Then read the card Why a black cloth gets hotter in the sun.
flow.say: Was your guess right? Both cloths had the same sun. So why did the black one melt its ice faster?
flow.kid: Was your guess right? Both cloths had the same sun. Why did the ice under the black cloth melt more?

ask.q: Why did the ice melt faster under the black cloth?
good: The black cloth took in more sunlight and got hotter.
The white cloth sent the light back, so it stayed cooler.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the evidence: 'The black cloth felt hotter, and its plate had more spoons of water.' Then add the words: black absorbs, or takes in, most of the light, and white reflects, or sends back, most of it.

check.q: You are going to the beach in Chennai in May. Which shirt will keep you coolest in the sun?
check.why: A white shirt reflects most of the sunlight, so it stays cooler, and loose cotton lets air move. If you chose the black shirt, remember that in the Black or White test the ice under the black cloth melted first.

experiments.title: The Damp Box: can air make a crisp papad soft?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put two halves of a crisp papad in two closed boxes. One box has damp air inside, like monsoon air. You find out whether air can carry water into food.
experiments.question: Does a crisp papad go soft in a box of damp air, even when it never touches water?
experiments.predict: Guess first. After half an hour, will the papad in the damp box still snap, or will it bend? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We break one papad into two halves, so both start the same. Both boxes are the same and both are closed. Neither half touches any water. The only difference is the cup of warm water in one box.
results_table: What happened when I bent it after 30 minutes?

materials.item: one crisp papad: a ready-roasted one from a packet, or an uncooked one that a grown-up has roasted in a microwave for about a minute and let cool
two steel dabbas with lids, big enough to hold a small cup and half a papad
a small steel cup of hot water from the tap or kettle, poured by a grown-up
two small plates or saucers that fit inside the dabbas

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water. Keep fingers away from the hot cup.

schedule.what: Guess, set up the two boxes, wait 30 minutes while doing something else, then test the two halves and talk about why.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Draw the two halves: one snapped and one bent, or however they came out.

setup.art: A crisp roasted papad being broken into two halves over a plate.
setup.caption: 1. Break a crisp papad into two halves.

setup.art: Two open steel dabbas: one with half a papad on a saucer and a small cup of steaming water beside it, the other with only half a papad on a saucer.
setup.caption: 2. One box gets a cup of hot water too. Close both lids.

setup.art: A child bending two papad halves: one snaps cleanly, the other bends softly.
setup.caption: 3. After 30 minutes, try to bend each half.

flow.do: 1. Take a crisp papad. 2. Your child snaps a tiny corner to hear the crack. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Hear the crack? It is crisp. In one box, the air will be damp, like monsoon air. Will this papad stay crisp in there? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Hear the snap? Will it stay crisp in damp air? Why?
flow.parent: Many children think nothing can happen unless the papad touches water. That is a good guess to test.

flow.do: 1. Break the papad into two halves. 2. Put each half on a small saucer inside a dabba. 3. A grown-up puts a small cup of hot water into one dabba, beside the saucer. 4. Close both lids.
flow.say: The papad must not touch the water. Only the air in the box is different.
flow.kid: Put one half in each box. Hot water goes in one box only. Close the lids.
flow.parent: Make sure the papad and the water cup do not touch. The hot water makes the air in the box very damp.

flow.do: Leave both boxes closed for 30 minutes. Play a game or read the story while you wait.
flow.say: Now we wait half an hour. What do you think is happening in the damp box?
flow.kid: Wait 30 minutes. What is happening in the box?
flow.parent: Papads differ. If the half from the damp box still snaps after 30 minutes, close the box and wait 30 more minutes before you bend it again.

flow.do: 1. Open both boxes. 2. Look at the inside of the lids. 3. Your child bends each papad half gently.
flow.say: Look under the lids first. What do you see? Now bend each half. Which one snaps?
flow.kid: Look under the lids. Now bend each half. Which one snaps?

ask.q: What was under the lid of the damp box?
good: Drops of water.
The lid was wet inside.

flow.parent: The half from the dry box should still snap. The half from the damp box should bend or feel leathery, or at least be less snappy. The drops under the lid show that the air carried water.

flow.do: Ask your child what they saw, and why they think it happened.
flow.say: The papad never touched the water. So how did it get soft?
flow.kid: The papad never touched the water. How did it go soft?

ask.q: Where did the water come from?
good: From the air in the box.
The hot water went into the air, and the papad soaked it up.

flow.parent: This is why papads, biscuits and salt go soft or lumpy in the monsoon. Monsoon air is humid: it holds a lot of water you cannot see.

check.q: In Mumbai in July, an open packet of biscuits is left on the table. What will happen to the biscuits?
check.why: In the monsoon the air is humid, and biscuits soak up water from the air. If you chose 'nothing', remember that the papad in the damp box went soft without touching the water.

activities.title: What Changed? Spot the season in old family photos
activities.context: In this activity you look at family photos taken in different months. You spot the clues that show the season.

materials.item: a grown-up's phone with photos from a few different months of the year, or a family photo album

schedule.what: Look at three photos from different months and find the season clues in each.

activities.record: Draw one photo, and circle the clue that shows its season.

setup.art: A mother and a girl looking at a phone together, with three small photos on the screen: a sunny beach, a rainy street and a family in sweaters.
setup.caption: 1. Find three photos from different months.

setup.art: A girl pointing at an umbrella in a photo on a phone screen.
setup.caption: 2. Find the clues that show the season.

flow.do: 1. Find three photos on your phone, one from April or May, one from July or August, and one from December or January. 2. Do not say the months yet.
flow.say: Here are three photos of us. They were taken at different times of the year. Look carefully.
flow.kid: Look at three photos. They are from different times of the year.
flow.parent: Photos taken outdoors or by a window show the most clues. Any photos will do.

flow.do: For each photo, ask your child to find clues: clothes, the sky, wet or dry roads, trees, fans, food, festivals.
flow.say: What are we wearing here? Is the road wet or dry? What is the sky like? Which season do you think this is? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the clothes and the sky. Which season is it? Why?

ask.q: What clue told you the season?
good: We are wearing sweaters, so it is winter.
There are puddles and umbrellas, so it is the monsoon.
Everyone is sweaty and in cotton, so it is summer.

flow.parent: Then tell your child the month each photo was taken. Was their guess right?

flow.do: Ask what changes from one season to the next.
flow.say: What changed between these photos? Name three things.
flow.kid: Name three things that changed.

check.q: In a photo, a boy is wearing a raincoat and there are puddles on the road. Which season is it?
check.why: A raincoat and puddles are clues for the rainy season, the monsoon. If you chose summer, look for clues of heat instead, like cotton clothes and bright, dry roads.

activities.title: Phone a Faraway Family: what season is it there?
activities.context: In this activity you call a relative or friend who lives in another part of India. You ask about their weather today, and compare it with yours.

materials.item: a phone, and a relative or family friend who lives in another city or state
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Write three questions, make the call, and compare their weather with yours.

activities.record: Make two columns: 'Here' and 'There'. Write or draw the answers to the three questions in each column.

setup.art: A girl on a video call with her aunt, who stands in bright sun while the girl's window shows rain.
setup.caption: 1. Call someone who lives far away.

setup.art: A page with two columns, 'Here' and 'There', and little drawings of rain on one side and a sun on the other.
setup.caption: 2. Write the answers in two columns.

flow.do: 1. Choose who to call. 2. Help your child write three questions: Is it hot or cool today? Is it raining? What are you wearing?
flow.say: Let us call someone who lives far away. What would you like to ask them about their weather?
flow.kid: Who shall we call? Write three questions about their weather.
flow.parent: Grandparents, cousins and family friends in other cities are perfect. If nobody lives far away, look up today's weather for another city on a phone together.

flow.do: Make the call. Your child asks the three questions and listens. Write down or draw the answers.
flow.say: Ask your questions. Listen carefully to the answers.
flow.kid: Ask your three questions. Listen. Draw the answers.

flow.do: Compare 'Here' and 'There'. Find both places on a map if you have one.
flow.say: Is their weather the same as ours today? Why might it be different?
flow.kid: Is their weather the same as ours? Why not?

ask.q: Why might the weather be different there?
good: They live far away.
The monsoon reaches some places first.
They live up in the mountains, where it is colder.

flow.parent: A good answer says the place is far away, or in the mountains, or by the sea. It is fine if the child just notices the difference.

activities.title: My Window in Three Seasons: a drawing
activities.context: In this activity you draw the view from your window three times: once in summer, once in the monsoon and once in winter.

materials.item: a sheet of paper folded into three parts
colour pencils or crayons

schedule.what: Look out of the window, then draw the same view in three seasons.

activities.record: Keep the drawing. Label each part with the season and the months.

setup.art: A sheet of paper folded into three columns, with a window frame drawn at the top of each.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a paper into three parts.

setup.art: The same window view drawn three times: a bright dry street, a rainy street with umbrellas, and a misty morning street.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the same view in summer, monsoon and winter.

flow.do: Look out of the window together for two minutes. Name what you see.
flow.say: Look out of the window. What can you see? A tree, a road, the sky, a shop?
flow.kid: Look out of the window. What can you see?

flow.do: Your child draws the same view three times, one in each part of the paper.
flow.say: Now draw this view three times. What would it look like in summer? In the monsoon? In winter?
flow.kid: Draw the view three times: summer, monsoon and winter.
flow.parent: Ask about details: Would the tree look the same? Would people carry umbrellas? Would the sky be bright, grey or misty?

flow.do: Look at the three pictures together.
flow.say: What changed in your three pictures? What stayed the same?
flow.kid: What changed? What stayed the same?

ask.q: What stayed the same in all three?
good: The building and the road.
The tree is still there, but with different leaves or flowers.

activities.title: One Minute of Listening: what does the season sound like?
activities.context: In this activity you sit by a window, close your eyes and listen for one minute. You count the sounds that tell you the season.

materials.item: a window you can open or sit near
a phone timer

schedule.what: Listen for one minute and count the season sounds.

activities.record: Write or draw each sound you heard. Put a star next to the ones that belong to one season.

setup.art: A boy sitting by an open window with his eyes closed and a hand cupped behind one ear.
setup.caption: 1. Sit by the window and close your eyes.

setup.art: A list on paper with small drawings: a bird, rain drops, a fan and a horn, with stars next to the bird and the rain.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the sounds you heard.

flow.do: 1. Sit by the window. 2. Set the timer for one minute. 3. Close your eyes and listen.
flow.say: Close your eyes. Listen for one minute. Count every sound you hear on your fingers.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Listen for one minute. Count the sounds.

flow.do: Name the sounds. Decide which ones belong to one season.
flow.say: What did you hear? Which sounds only come in one season?
flow.kid: What did you hear? Which sounds come in only one season?
flow.parent: Season sounds include the koel's 'koo-oo' in summer, rain and frogs in the monsoon, and kite-flying shouts in Gujarat in January. A fan or a cooler running is a summer sound too.

activities.title: The Papad Weather Test: is today's air damp or dry?
activities.context: In this activity you leave a piece of crisp papad on a plate in the room. If it goes soft, the air is humid. Try it in different seasons.

materials.item: a small piece of crisp papad: a ready-roasted one, or an uncooked one that a grown-up has roasted in a microwave and let cool
a plate

schedule.what: Put the papad out in the morning, and test it after two hours.

activities.record: Write the date, the season, and whether the papad snapped or bent.

setup.art: A small piece of crisp papad on a plate on a table, with a clock showing 9 o'clock.
setup.caption: 1. Leave a crisp papad piece on a plate.

setup.art: The same table with the clock showing 11 o'clock, and a child bending the papad piece.
setup.caption: 2. After two hours, bend it. Does it snap?

flow.do: Put a small piece of crisp papad on a plate in the room in the morning.
flow.say: We will leave this papad out for two hours. Will it stay crisp today? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Leave the papad on a plate. Will it stay crisp?

flow.do: After two hours, your child bends the papad. Write down if it snapped or bent.
flow.say: Bend it gently. Does it snap or bend? So is today's air damp or dry?
flow.kid: Bend the papad. Snap or bend? Is the air damp or dry?
flow.parent: In the monsoon, and in coastal cities like Chennai, Mumbai and Kolkata, the papad may start to bend instead of snapping. If it still snaps, leave the next piece out for a whole day. In a dry winter or summer in Jaipur or Delhi, it may stay crisp all day.

projects.title: Our Family Season Calendar
projects.context: In this project you make a big calendar of the year for your home. You mark the seasons where you live, and the family's festivals, foods and clothes for each month.

materials.item: a big sheet of paper, or four sheets taped together
a printed calendar of this year, or a grown-up's phone calendar
colour pencils or crayons: orange, blue and green

schedule.what: Draw 12 boxes for the 12 months, write the names, and colour each month by its season where you live.
Ask the family about festivals, foods and clothes in each month, and draw one thing in each box. Then count the months in each season.

projects.record: The finished calendar on the wall, and a sentence at the bottom: 'Where we live, the longest season is ___.'

setup.art: A big sheet with 12 boxes in three rows of four, each labelled with a month from January to December.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 12 boxes, one for each month.

setup.art: The 12 boxes coloured orange for summer, blue for the monsoon and green for winter.
setup.caption: 2. Colour each month by its season.

setup.art: Small drawings in the boxes: kites in January, mangoes in May, an umbrella in July, a lamp for Deepavali in October or November.
setup.caption: 3. Draw one family thing in each month.

flow.do: 1. Draw 12 boxes on the big sheet. 2. Your child copies the names of the months from the calendar, one in each box.
flow.say: A year has 12 months. Let us write them in order, starting with January.
flow.kid: Write the 12 months in order. Start with January.

flow.do: Colour each month: orange for summer, blue for the monsoon, green for winter. Decide together for your own city.
flow.say: Which months are hot here? Which are rainy? Which are cool? Let us colour them.
flow.kid: Colour hot months orange, rainy months blue, cool months green.
flow.parent: Use your own city. In Chennai, colour October to December blue. In Mumbai, June to September. In Bengaluru, rain falls in many months, with the most in September and October. There is no single right answer for all of India.

flow.do: On day 2, ask the people you live with, or call a relative, about each month. Draw one festival, food or piece of clothing in each box.
flow.say: Let us ask our family and friends. What do we eat, wear or celebrate in each month?
flow.kid: Ask your family. What happens in each month? Draw one thing in each box.
flow.parent: Festivals that move with the moon calendar, like Deepavali or Eid, can fall in different months in different years. Draw them where they fall this year.

flow.do: Count the boxes of each colour. Write the numbers at the bottom.
flow.say: How many orange months? How many blue? How many green? Which season is longest here?
flow.kid: Count the orange, blue and green months. Which season is longest?

check.q: In Mumbai, the monsoon lasts from June to September. How many months is that?
check.why: June, July, August and September: count them on your fingers. That is 4 months. If you said 3, check that you counted both June and September.

challenges.title: Keep the Papad Crisp in the Monsoon
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the monsoon, damp air makes papads go soft. Your job is to design a way to keep a papad crisp in a damp box.
challenges.problem: Can you keep half a papad crisp for 30 minutes inside a damp box, like the one in the Damp Box test? The other half of the papad sits in the same box with no protection, to compare.
constraints: Use only things from home: a dabba, a plastic bag, a rubber band, paper, a spoon of uncooked rice or salt.
Both papad halves must stay inside the damp box, with the cup of hot water.
You may wrap or cover the papad, but you must be able to take it out and bend it.
materials: a crisp papad, broken in half (a ready-roasted one, or an uncooked one a grown-up has roasted in a microwave and let cool)
one big steel dabba with a lid
a small cup of hot water, poured by a grown-up
a small plastic bag, or a small dabba with a tight lid
general: Put the papad inside a small dabba with a tight lid, inside the damp box, so the damp air cannot reach it.
Seal the papad in a small plastic bag with a rubber band.
This is why families store papads, biscuits and chips in airtight tins in the monsoon.
creative: Put a spoon of uncooked rice in the small dabba with the papad. Some people believe dry rice soaks up damp from the air. Does it help?
Wrap the papad in a few layers of newspaper. Does paper keep the damp out, or soak it up?
challenges.your_turn: Try your own design. After 30 minutes, bend the papad. Does it snap? If it bends, think about how the damp air got in, and try again.

setup.art: A table with a crisp papad half, a small steel dabba, a plastic bag, a rubber band and a spoon of rice.
setup.caption: 1. Collect your things.

setup.art: A big open steel dabba with a cup of steaming water inside and a small closed dabba holding a papad beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Put the protected papad and the bare papad in the damp box. Close the lid.

setup.art: A child bending a papad that snaps with a crack, and smiling.
setup.caption: 3. After 30 minutes, test it. Does it snap?

flow.do: Read the challenge with your child. Show the things they may use.
flow.say: Damp air made the papad soft. How could you keep the damp air away from it? Why do you think that will work?
flow.kid: Damp air makes papads soft. How can you keep the damp air out? Why?

flow.do: Your child builds the design for one papad half. A grown-up puts the hot water cup in the big dabba. Put the protected half and the bare half inside, not touching the cup, and close the lid.
flow.say: Build your idea. Then put it in the damp box and close the lid.
flow.kid: Build your idea. Put it in the damp box. Close the lid.

flow.do: Wait 30 minutes with the lid closed. Play a game or read the story while you wait.
flow.say: Which half do you think will stay crisp?
flow.kid: Wait 30 minutes. Which half will stay crisp?

flow.do: Take out both halves and bend each one. Talk about what worked.
flow.say: Does it snap? What kept the damp air out? What would you change?
flow.kid: Bend both halves. Which one snaps? What worked?
flow.parent: A tight lid or a sealed bag usually works best, because the damp air cannot get in. The bare half shows what damp air does. If both halves still snap, your papad may take longer to go soft: wait 30 more minutes.

challenges.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water.

opts: A part of the year with its own kind of weather
quiz.why: A season lasts many weeks and comes back every year. One rainy day is just weather.

quiz.p: In most of India, which season comes right after summer?
quiz.why: In most of India, the monsoon rains come after the hot summer, from June.

quiz.p: Which of these changes from summer to winter?
opts: The number of days in a week
The colour of the sky at night
quiz.why: People change their clothes with the seasons. A week always has 7 days.

quiz.p: Why do clothes take so long to dry in the monsoon?
opts: The air is humid, full of water we cannot see
quiz.why: Humid air already holds a lot of water, so wet clothes dry slowly. The Damp Box test showed that air can carry water.

quiz.p: Where does the monsoon rain usually arrive first?
quiz.why: The monsoon rain usually reaches Kerala around the first of June, then moves north.

quiz.p: When does Chennai get most of its rain?
quiz.why: Chennai gets most of its rain from the northeast monsoon, from October to December.

quiz.p: Why does a white cloth stay cooler in the sun?
opts: It reflects most of the sunlight
It has no sunlight on it

quiz.p: Why do male frogs croak loudly in the monsoon?

roots.context: We have sorted the year into seasons and watched ice melt under two cloths in the sun. Now we ask what the Black or White test tells us about sunlight, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the same sunshine, the ice under the black cloth melted first. The black cloth took in most of the light, and that light became heat. The white cloth sent most of the light away again. So how hot a thing gets in the summer sun depends on how much of the light it takes in.
deep_truth.habit: We think of summer heat as something in the air, the same for everything around us. But in the Black or White test, two cloths side by side in the same sun ended up at very different temperatures. The heat came from the light each one took in.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Black or White test, the black cloth felt hotter after 10 minutes, and its plate held more spoons of melted ice after 15 minutes. Both cloths had the same sun for the same time.

three.who_am_i: You take in sunlight too. Your skin, your hair and your clothes all absorb some of it and turn it into warmth.
three.what_is_life: Frogs, koels, trees and people all sense the season and change what they do: they call, flower, sow seeds or change their clothes.
three.what_is_this_world: The same Sun shines on all of India, yet one place is rainy and another dry, one roof hot and another cool. What each place and thing does with the light makes the difference.

roots.thread: The same Sun lights the whole of India. Each thing it falls on takes in a different share of the light: a black road takes in a lot, a white wall little. Land also warms faster than the sea, and that is one idea for what brings the monsoon wind.

how_we_found_out.story: People in hot places have worn white and pale clothes for a very long time. Benjamin Franklin, an American printer and scientist, tested why. In the early 1760s he wrote about it in a letter to Mary Stevenson, a young woman in London who studied science with him by letter. He had laid small squares of cloth of many colours on snow on a sunny morning. A few hours later, the black square had sunk deepest into the snow, because it had melted the most. The white square stayed on top. Franklin said people in hot, sunny places should wear white. After this, many people believed that black clothes always make you hotter. In 1980, the scientists Amiram Shkolnik, Virginia Finch and their team tested people of the Bedouin desert tribes, who wear loose black robes. The black robe did get hotter on the outside. But the person inside gained about the same heat as in a white robe. Air moving under the loose robe carried the extra heat away. So colour matters, and so does how clothes fit and how the air moves.
how_we_found_out.who: Benjamin Franklin, who wrote to Mary Stevenson, and later Amiram Shkolnik, Virginia Finch and their team
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That black clothes always make the wearer hotter in the sun. A black cloth does take in more sunlight, but the 1980 desert study showed that a loose black robe let moving air carry the extra heat away, so the person inside was no hotter.
